skill.name: Idioms: the meaning isn't the words
skill.why: Idioms are everywhere in talk and stories. Taken literally, they make no sense.
skill.how: Notice when the words can't be literally true. Use the story around it.

beats.say: Some sayings don't mean what the words say.
Did Mo drop a tin of beans? Not this time!
Check the story around it for clues.
beats.show: Mo **spilled the beans** about Tully's **surprise** party.

beats.say: So it means Mo told a secret. That's an idiom.
Aussies love them. 'Spit the dummy' means throw a tantrum.
beats.show: Zed **spat the dummy** when he lost.

creature.name: Archiom
creature.blurb: An archerfish that spits sayings instead of water. Take them literally and you'll miss. Read the clues around them and you'll hit the target.

encounters.frame: Zed is telling the crew about the new game quiz at school. The Archiom is listening from the bucket.
encounters.text: On Friday, our class had a quiz about video games. Mr Lee wrote ten questions on the board. Most kids groaned. Zed grinned. He knew every single answer. encounters.success: It was very easy. Zed knew every answer and finished in two minutes.

options.text: The quiz was very hard.
options.reason: Zed knew every answer and finished in two minutes. It wasn't hard for him.

encounters.frame: Tully is reading out a story from the Space Club newsletter. The Archiom keeps splashing.
encounters.text: The Space Club had spent six weeks building a model rocket. On launch day, they carried it out to the middle of the footy oval. 'We haven't checked the wind yet, and Mr Ford is still mowing the far end of the oval.' Jasper's finger froze just above the button. Ms Nguyen licked her finger and held it up. Then she waited until Mr Ford had parked his mower behind the shed. 'Right,' she said. 'Now you can launch.' The rocket shot up so high that it disappeared into a cloud. Nobody has found it yet.

encounters.text: This term, Kenji decided to learn the guitar, the drums, the trumpet and the violin, all at once. He also joined the choir and signed up to play a solo at the end-of-term concert. encounters.frame: The crew wrote their diaries. The Archiom wants to sort out what they meant.
encounters.prompt: Match each idiom to what it means.
encounters.success: The clue in each sentence told you the meaning, even if you'd never heard the idiom.

items.text: Mum has been flat out at work all week. She hasn't had one lunch break.
items.reason: 'Flat out' is Aussie for very busy, not lying flat. No lunch break is the clue.

items.text: Wren has been run off her feet at the rescue centre, with ten new joeys to feed.
items.reason: 'Run off her feet' means so busy she never stops. Ten joeys is a lot of work.

items.reason: 'Child's play' means so easy that a little kid could do it.

items.reason: 'A breeze' isn't a wind here. Finishing first with every answer right is the clue.

items.reason: His heart didn't really move. Hardly daring to breathe is the clue.

encounters.frame: Gus is telling the crew about his aunt's wedding. The Archiom thinks it sounds fancy.
encounters.text: My aunt got married in a fancy hotel in the city. Before we went in, Mum gave me a serious look. 'Mind your p's and q's tonight,' she said. So I did. I said please and thank you to every waiter. I put my napkin on my lap and chewed with my mouth closed. I didn't burp once, not even after the fizzy drink. I even asked the lady next to me how her day had been. Then she asked me about my hobbies, so I told her all about my fish-guts experiment. She moved to another table. Mum says I did really well until dessert.
encounters.prompt: What does Mum mean by 'Mind your p's and q's'?
encounters.success: Use your best manners. So Gus says please and thank you, and doesn't burp once.

options.text: Use your very best manners.
Stay quiet and don't talk to anyone.
options.reason: Gus chats to the lady next to him, and Mum says he did well. What else did he do?

options.text: Eat everything that is on your plate.
options.reason: Mum never mentions food. Think about please, thank you and no burping.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote about the first morning of reef camp. The Archiom was there too.
encounters.text: On the first morning of reef camp, twelve kids who had never met before sat in a circle on the deck of the dive boat. Nobody said a word. Some stared at their flippers, and one boy pretended to read the safety sign for ten whole minutes. The silence was awful. Then Mo, who had come along as the camp cook, stood up with a plate of his fish-finger custard. 'Who wants to be brave first?' he asked. One girl laughed, then another. Soon everyone was arguing about whether fish fingers belonged anywhere near custard, and swapping stories about the worst food they had ever eaten. By lunchtime, the whole group was chatting and laughing together. The camp leader told Mo later that he had really broken the ice. Mo was so pleased that he made a second batch. Nobody ate that one either, but it gave them something else to talk about.
encounters.prompt: What does the camp leader mean when she says Mo broke the ice?
encounters.success: He got everyone relaxed and talking. The silence ended, and soon all the kids were chatting happily.

options.text: He made the awkward silence even worse.
options.reason: After Mo's custard, everyone laughs and starts chatting. He ended the silence.

options.text: He got everyone relaxed and talking to each other.
He smashed the ice in the drinks cooler.
options.reason: There's no ice in the story. The leader is talking about how the kids started chatting.

options.text: He started an argument that upset the group.
options.reason: They argued about custard, but in a fun way. By lunchtime they were all chatting happily.

encounters.frame: Tully is telling the crew about Sunday lunch at her nan's. The Archiom is under the table.
encounters.text: Every Sunday, my whole family squeezes around Nan's dining table for roast chicken. Last Sunday, my little cousin Archie decided he was a comedian. When Nan put the gravy on the table, he said it was the colour of swamp water. When Uncle Ray told a story about his fishing trip, Archie yawned loudly and said, 'Wake me up when the fish gets away.' Then he poked Nan's famous pudding with his spoon and asked if it was meant to be that colour. Everyone went quiet. Nan put down her spoon, looked at Archie over the top of her glasses and said, 'Pull your head in, young man.' Archie went bright red. He said sorry to Nan, ate two bowls of pudding without another word, and even offered to do the dishes. Nan gave him a third bowl. That's how you know she has forgiven you. Archie has been very polite ever since. Mostly.
encounters.prompt: What does Nan mean when she tells Archie to pull his head in?
encounters.success: Stop being cheeky and rude. Archie had been insulting the food and the stories, so Nan told him off.

options.text: Duck down so you don't bump your head.
options.reason: Archie is sitting at the table. Nothing could bump his head. Nan is cross about his cheek.

options.text: Stop daydreaming and pay attention.
options.reason: Archie isn't daydreaming. Listen to the comments he keeps making.

options.text: Stop being cheeky and rude to everyone.
Think harder before you answer a question.
options.reason: Nobody asked Archie a question. What has Archie been saying to everyone?

encounters.frame: Tully wrote up the Year 6 relay race for the school newsletter. The Archiom is still laughing.
encounters.text: The Year 6 relay was the last race of the athletics carnival, and the Blue team was in the lead. Ruby was running the final leg. She stood in her lane, bouncing on her toes, waiting for Eli to bring her the baton. When Eli was still halfway down the track, Ruby heard the crowd cheering and thought it was for her. She took off, sprinting as hard as she could, all the way to the finish line. She crossed it with her arms in the air, before Eli had even reached the changeover. Then she turned around and saw that her hands were empty. Eli was standing at the changeover, holding out the baton to nobody. 'You jumped the gun,' said Coach Ellis, shaking her head. Ruby had to walk all the way back and run the leg again. Blue came third, but Ruby still says she ran the fastest leg of the day, twice.
encounters.prompt: What does Coach Ellis mean when she says Ruby jumped the gun?
encounters.success: Ruby went too soon. She ran before Eli gave her the baton.

options.text: Ruby leapt over the starter's gun on the track.
options.reason: Nobody jumps over anything. When did Ruby leave, and did she have the baton?

options.text: Ruby started running before she should have.
Ruby ran much more slowly than the others.
options.reason: Ruby sprinted as hard as she could. Speed wasn't the problem. Look at when she ran.

options.text: Ruby got such a fright that she ran away.
options.reason: Ruby wasn't scared. She thought the cheering meant it was her turn to run.

encounters.frame: Indi found this letter in the Soggy Biscuit's mailbag. The Archiom is drying it out.
encounters.text: Dear Aunty Bec, Guess what? My team won the Junior Space Challenge! We had to design a base for astronauts living on the Moon, with enough water, food and air for four people for a whole year, and then present it to a panel of real scientists. The competition was on Friday morning, and on Monday we still hadn't finished. So for the last four nights, we burned the midnight oil. Every evening after dinner, the three of us crowded around the kitchen table at Priya's house, surrounded by cardboard tubes and glue, working until nearly midnight while her parents brought us cups of hot chocolate. The lights were on the whole time, so we could see every tiny piece. On Thursday night, Priya's dad found us asleep on top of the model, with glue in our hair. We slept in on Friday morning and nearly missed the bus, but we made it, and the judges said our water recycling tank was the cleverest design they had seen all year. The prize is a trip to the space centre in the holidays. Mum says next time we should start earlier, and she is probably right. Priya's dad says next time we should use less glue. Love, Ava

encounters.success: They worked late into the night. Every evening they worked until nearly midnight to finish the base.

options.text: They lit oil lamps, because the power had gone out.
options.reason: Ava says the lights were on the whole time. Nothing was really burning.

options.text: They got up very early each morning to work.
options.reason: They worked in the evenings, until nearly midnight. They even slept in on Friday.

options.text: They wasted a lot of time and energy on the project.
options.reason: Their hard work paid off: the judges loved their design. Nothing was wasted.

When he carried it out to the table, it was black on top and smoking slightly, and the whole house smelled of smoke. Nobody said a word about it. Everyone burst out laughing, including Mo, and Nan said it was the most memorable birthday cake she had ever had. They ordered pizza.

items.text: After the sixth failed experiment, Gus called it quits, packed away his test tubes and went to bed.
items.reason: 'Called it quits' means he stopped. Packing away the test tubes is the clue.

items.text: After an hour of missed kicks, Tully threw in the towel and went inside, leaving the ball on the grass.
items.reason: There's no towel. Leaving the ball behind shows she gave up.

items.text: Zed knew he was in deep water when his teacher found the drawing of her and asked to see his parents.
items.reason: He wasn't swimming. A teacher asking to see your parents is a clue.

items.text: Wren bit the bullet and rang the vet, even though she was dreading the news.
items.reason: There's no bullet. Dreading the news but ringing anyway is the clue.

items.text: Mo took the plunge and put his name down for the talent show, though his knees were knocking.
items.reason: Nobody dived anywhere. Knocking knees show he was scared but did it anyway.

items.text: The Reef Rays win a grand final once in a blue moon. Their last win was in 1978.
items.reason: Blue moons are rare. A last win in 1978 is the clue.

encounters.frame: Maxx Vantablack is live, and he is not happy. Zed is recording it for evidence.
encounters.text: Vantafam, Maxx here, and today I need to talk about something serious. Some of you have been leaving comments saying my rescues are fake. Fake! Me! After everything I've done for the Creatures of this archipelago! One person said the swamp behind me is painted on a board. Another said they could see a camera crew in the reflection of my sunnies. Someone even said the Creature I rescued last week had a price tag on its tail. Come on, guys, fair crack of the whip! I have spent six years building this channel. I have rescued more Creatures than anyone in history, probably. I deserve a chance to show you what I really do before you start writing nasty comments about me. So this week, I'm doing something special. I'm going to film a rescue from start to finish, with no editing at all, so you can all see for yourselves. Well, a little bit of editing. For the lighting. And the sound. And maybe a couple of the bits in the middle. But apart from that, totally real. Smash that heart button if you believe in me, and remember, two Xs, because one X is for losers. Stay gold!
encounters.prompt: What does Maxx mean when he says 'fair crack of the whip'?
encounters.success: Give me a fair chance. Maxx says he deserves a chance to show what he really does.

options.text: Punish the people who write mean comments.
options.reason: Maxx wants something for himself, not punishment for others. He says he deserves a chance.

options.text: Hurry up and make up your minds about me.
options.reason: Maxx wants viewers to wait and watch first, before they start writing comments.

options.text: Give me a fair chance before you judge me.
Stop making jokes about my rescue videos.
options.reason: The comments aren't jokes. People think his rescues are fake, and he wants a fair chance.

encounters.frame: Tully is telling the crew about a family mystery. The Archiom has its fins crossed.
encounters.text: In my grandpa's lounge room, there is a glass cabinet full of footy trophies, and right in the middle stands the biggest one of all, the 1978 Mangrove Cup. It has a crack running all the way down one side, and someone has glued the handle back on, a bit crooked. Nobody in my family will say how it happened. Last weekend, while Grandpa was out walking his dog, I asked Gran about it. She was sitting on the back step, shelling peas. She stopped for a moment, looked at the cabinet through the window, and then went back to her peas. 'Some things are better left alone, love,' she said. 'Let sleeping dogs lie.' I tried asking Uncle Ray instead, but he suddenly remembered he had to mow the lawn, even though he had mowed it that morning. Aunty Jo just laughed until she had to sit down. When Grandpa came home with the dog, I opened my mouth to ask him, and Gran gave me a very stern look. So I closed it again. I still don't know what happened to that trophy, but I have a feeling Grandpa does. And I have a feeling it's a very good story.
encounters.prompt: What does Gran mean when she says 'Let sleeping dogs lie'?
encounters.success: Leave it alone and don't stir up an old problem. Gran says some things are better left alone.

options.text: Don't wake up Grandpa's dog while it's resting.
options.reason: Grandpa's dog is out walking with him, not asleep. Gran is talking about the trophy.

options.text: Leave the old story alone and don't bring it up.
Wait until tomorrow morning and then ask again.
options.reason: Gran doesn't say to ask later. She says some things are better left alone.

options.text: Go and ask Grandpa, because he knows the truth.
options.reason: Gran gives Tully a look to stop her asking Grandpa. She wants it left alone.
